newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM braces for new attack from parliament.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM braces for new attack from parliament.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin faces a new attack in parliament on Tuesday when the upper chamber meets to discuss his economic record amid strikes and discontent.
Chernomyrdin has already been forced to defend his policies from fierce criticism in the lower house, where he is fighting hard for approval of the government's 1997 spending plans.

The 58-year-old prime minister, a loyal ally to President Boris Yeltsin, tried to head off an assault in the Federation Council upper house by meeting deputies on Monday but faces a grilling if he shows up to defend himself on Tuesday.
"We have to solve problems and untie knots together," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying at talks with a delegation from the Federation Council.
"We must not be divided. But it is the government's lot to adopt unpopular measures."
Chernomyrdin has held on to power through one crisis after another since becoming prime minister in December 1992.

Although a non-confidence motion in the government is unlikely, Chernomyrdin is again facing a major challenge and bearing the brunt of the criticism while Yeltsin, 65, is out of the Kremlin recovering from heart surgery.
The opposition-dominated lower house, the State Duma, has long criticised Chernomyrdin's pro-reform policies and has made several unsuccessful bids to oust him.

The Federation Council has traditionally been more compliant but turned against him last Wednesday when, citing illness, he ignored a request to go to the chamber to explain the failure to pay a huge backlog of pension and wages.
Some Council members, drawn from Russia's regional leaders, questioned last week whether Chernomyrdin should stay on.

"You've got to go to Chernomyrdin and ask him if he has the will and the courage to work on in this post or not," Boris Nemtsov, the liberal governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, told Council speaker Yegor Stroyev during a parliamentary debate.
Chernomyrdin said on Monday he was now ready to go to the Federation Council to discuss the country's problems but did not make clear whether this meant he would attend Tuesday's session.

Hundreds of thousands of coalminers went on strike last week because many of them have not been paid for months. Coal companies say many miners have gone back to work but trade union leaders sid on Monday the protest would continue.

Chernomyrdin says the problems with paying wages and pensions, which Yeltsin promised to settle during his election campaign earlier this year, are partly due to widespread tax evasion which has left the government short of money.
The Kremlin faces a host of other problems, not least gains by the opposition in the latest of a series of elections of regional governors at the weekend.

Candidates backed by the communist-led opposition won four of the 10 governor's posts that were decided on Sunday and Kremlin-backed candidates won only two. Four other elections will be decided in second-round voting later this year.
The Kremlin shrugged off the setbacks by saying it could work with most of the successful opposition candidates.

Yeltsin moved on Monday to a state residence west of Moscow where he will spend the "final stage" of his rehabilitation after his heart operation on November 5. Stroyev said last week the president would be back in the Kremlin by December 25.
